# On Reading Adam's Poem

Adam, I write to you as one poet to another, having spent time with the work you've shared. Your verses move through a landscape saturated with blue—image upon image, metaphor folding into metaphor until the language itself seems to shimmer. There is real craft here, a sensibility attuned to color and to the layered ways meaning can be suggested rather than stated.

Yet as I read, I find myself convinced that you carry within you a personal history capable of deepening this poem well beyond its figurative surface. The metaphors are beautiful, but they gesture toward something lived, something true, that I suspect you have not fully let into the lines. The poem could reach further if it drew from that well.

I want to be clear, though, that I understand why you might resist. Grief has its own logic, and sometimes what a poem needs is not raw fact but invention—a constructed image, even a mirage, that offers the necessary distance. Perspective can require a certain artifice. I accept that you may need these imagined figures to see clearly, or to survive the seeing.

Still, I keep returning to one question: what grounds the "we" in your poem? That collective pronoun carries weight, and I feel it must rest on something solid. A "we" cannot float untethered; it asks to be anchored in a relationship, a shared moment, a bond the reader can trust. Tell me what holds it in place.

And then, rereading once more, I begin to understand. I can see how another poet's "you" and "I"—those intimate pronouns from a voice you've clearly absorbed—have found their way into your own work. That influence is present here, woven into your speaker's stance, shaping the very way this poem addresses and imagines its subject. Recognizing it, I read your lines differently, and with new appreciation for the conversation you are quietly having across the page.
outputs.L4:
# On the Craft: A Letter to Adam

Adam, I have been thinking again about what it is we do when we set words against the blank of the page. You, of all people, will understand this preoccupation—you who have wrestled with the line, who have felt the pull between saying too much and saying nothing at all.

Consider the metaphor. It is our oldest instrument, this act of carrying one thing across into another, and yet how easily it becomes a vanity. When I reach for an image, I feel the temptation to dazzle, to make the comparison so unexpected that the reader gasps at my cleverness rather than at the world I meant to reveal. But the metaphor that announces itself too loudly has already failed. It has become invention for its own sake, a performance of ingenuity that forgets the thing it was meant to illuminate.

And then there is the matter of our words themselves—their private histories. Every poet carries a personal etymology, a set of meanings that certain words have accrued through the accidents of a life. To me, a word may be freighted with associations you could never guess; to you, the same word opens onto a landscape I will never see. This is both the intimacy and the isolation of what we do. We write believing our meanings will carry across, though we know that each word arrives at the reader trailing his own memories, not ours.

Think, too, of the pronouns—those small, treacherous words. When I write *we*, whom do I presume to include? I gather you and myself and some imagined community into a single gesture, and in doing so I risk a presumption I have not earned. When I write *you*, am I addressing you, Adam, or the reader I cannot see, or some absent figure I am only pretending to speak to? And the *I*—that most seductive of pronouns—how quickly it swells with conviction, how readily it mistakes its own voice for truth. These little words are the joints on which the whole poem turns, and we handle them too carelessly.

Here, then, is the observation I most wanted to share with you. The finest poetry, I have come to believe, is not the most inventive, nor the most impassioned. It is, rather, the poetry that manages its language *without too much invention or conviction*. This is the rarest quality of all. Too much invention, and the poem becomes a display of artifice, admiring itself in the mirror of its own novelty. Too much conviction, and it hardens into sermon, insisting upon a certainty that authentic feeling never possesses. Both are failures of restraint.

The delicate art lies in the balance—in holding the impulse to invent against the discipline to withhold, in tempering conviction with the honest hesitation of a mind still thinking. The poem that achieves this seems, paradoxically, both crafted and unforced, both made and found. It bears the marks of art without pretending to be anything other than the record of a genuine attempt to see.

This is what I aspire to, Adam, and what I so rarely reach. To write with enough invention to make the familiar strange, but not so much that I forget the familiar. To write with enough conviction to mean what I say, but not so much that I stop listening. Between artifice and authenticity there runs a narrow path, and the whole of our craft, I think, consists in learning to walk it.

Write back when you can. Tell me if I have this wrong.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem addressed to a fellow poet named Adam, reflecting on his poems and using metaphors about language, pronouns, and the craft of poetry itself.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Adam, Who Writes

You who parse the world in careful grammar,
who know a pronoun is a small door swinging—
*I* the hinge, *you* the threshold,
*we* the room where two lamps burn as one.

I have read your poems, Adam,
the way one reads a river:
not for the water but the way it holds
each syllable of light before releasing it.

You understand that language is a borrowed coat,
too large for any single shoulder,
that every noun once wore
the warm skin of a living thing.

When you write *stone*, I feel the weight.
When you write *bird*, something opens
in the cage behind my ribs
and will not settle.

This is the craft: to make the word
a window and not a wall,
to let the white space breathe
like the pause between two heartbeats.

You name yourself in every line—
not the *I* that struts and postures,
but the quieter self, the listener,
the one who lets the poem arrive.

So here, Adam, is my clumsy answer,
this letter made of the same clay
we both keep working with our thumbs:
imperfect, human, trying to hold light.

Keep the door swinging.
Keep the pronouns kind.
The whole tribe of us who love the word
is warmer for your making.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary free-verse poem that meditates on the "speaker" and "you" in poetry, weaving in themes of anxiety, metaphor, and pronouns like "we" and "I."
counterfactuals.output:
# Grammar of the Anxious

Let me begin with *I*,
that thin vertical stroke,
a lighthouse mistaking itself
for the storm it warns against.

The textbooks say
the *speaker* is not the poet—
a courtesy, a small mercy,
a mask I hold up
to my own trembling face
and call it craft.

But you know.

*You*—
second person, the accused,
the beloved, the reader
leaning too close to the page
like it might exhale.
I built you out of pronouns
because I could not say *him*,
could not say *the one who left*,
could not say the name
that still lives in my mouth
like a swallowed key.

Here is my anxiety,
dressed as metaphor:
a house with too many doors,
a phone that rings inside a dream,
the ocean rehearsing
its one gray argument
against the shore.

See how I did that?
Turned the shaking into weather.
Turned the panic into tide.
This is what we do—

and *we*, now,
the warmest lie of all,
the pronoun that pretends
you and I are standing
in the same wrecked kitchen
at 3 a.m.,
both of us afraid,
both of us awake.

Maybe that's the only truth
a poem can hold:
not *I* confessing,
not *you* forgiving,
but *we*—
this fragile syntax
where two solitudes
agree, for the length of a line,
to breathe.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ars poetica—a poem about poetry—that critiques and admires another poet's work, mentioning specific craft choices like homonyms, figures of speech, and over-determined moves.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ars Poetica with Marginalia**

I admire how you hinged the whole first stanza
on *bough* and *bow*—the tree limb and the surrender,
the way an ear must choose and, choosing, breaks.
That's craft: to let a homonym do the labor
two lines refused, to make the sound a fork
in the road the meaning takes.

But then the *heart like a wounded bird* arrives,
and I want to close the book. You know this bird.
It has been dying in our hands for centuries,
its little metaphor of blood and feather
worn smooth as a doorknob, turned by everyone,
opening nothing.

Still—the poem recovers. Section three,
where you let the metaphor collapse on purpose,
where the vehicle admits it cannot carry
the tenor's weight, and grief just sits there, *grief*,
unfigured, plain: that's braver than the swan
you smuggled in on page two, over-determined,

its neck already curved into a question mark
before you asked. You telegraph your endings.
I see the gun in the first act, the loaded
symbol, and I wait the whole poem through
for it to go off exactly when it does.
Surprise me. Load the gun and pour a drink from it.

What I keep is smaller: how you rhymed
*given* against *forgiven* without a sound
of triumph, slant enough to seem like accident,
the mercy hidden in the money of the mouth.
That is the thing I'd steal, if I could steal it—
the figure that refuses to perform,

the trope that turns its face against the reader,
the way you sometimes let a line just *stop*
before its music finishes the thought,
trusting the silence more than the device.
You are best when you distrust yourself. Do that.
The rest is *bough*. The rest is *bow*. Break there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental, conversational poem directed at another writer, blending praise and gentle critique about how they use metaphor, pronouns, and personal etymology in their verse.
counterfactuals.output:
# Notes Toward a Reading, Left in Your Mailbox

Listen—

you do this thing with *I*
where it opens like a door
that turns out to be a mirror
that turns out to be a window
someone else is standing at,

and I love it, mostly.

Mostly I love how your metaphors
arrive already apologizing,
how a river in your work
is never just water
but also your grandmother's name
misspelled on an immigration form,
also the sound *th* makes
when it forgets to be a *d*.

That's the good stuff.
Etymology as personal weather.

But—and I say this
the way you'd tell a friend
there's basil in their teeth,
which is to say: *because* I want you
walking into the next room beautiful—

sometimes the *you* in your poems
is doing seventeen jobs
and none of them get dental.
Is it me? Is it God?
Is it the ex? The reader?
The version of yourself
you keep almost forgiving?

I want to know
which *you* I'm being.

And the metaphors—
you stack them
like someone afraid of silence,
tenor on vehicle on tenor
until the little wagon of the image
can't move for all the freight.
One clean image, love,
can carry a whole grief across a border.
You don't have to hire the whole caravan.

Here's what I'm really saying:

your language *knows* something
your poems keep interrupting.
When you let a word
just be its own strange animal—
*"salt, which my mouth learned before it learned to lie"*—
I forget I'm reading.
I'm just there,
in the kitchen of the sentence,
being fed.

So this is me,
sliding this under your door,
signing it with a pronoun
we haven't invented yet,

the one that means
*I am arguing with you
because I plan to keep reading you
for a very long time.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of one poet speaking to another, exploring anxiety, the mechanics of poetic figures, and the tension between invention and sincerity.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Reading Your Latest, and Failing to Reply

Forgive me, friend—I've drafted this twelve times.
Each version wore a better coat than the last,
each simile I hung like borrowed chimes
to make my hollow ringing sound long-cast

in bronze. You'd catch it. You always catch the seam
where feeling ends and craftwork starts to show,
the way a tailor sees another's dream
of tailoring: the stitch, the practiced flow.

Here is my trouble. When I write *I ache*,
I watch my hand reach past the ache to find
the figure that will make the ache well-made—
and something honest dies to leave behind

a thing more shapely than the thing it meant.
Is that a lie? Or is the lie the raw
unmetered cry, which, being unrestrained,
mistakes its noise for truth, its hurt for law?

You taught me metaphor is how we cross
the water without drowning—carrying
the self on someone else's back. The cost
is never being wholly what we sing.

So take this anxious, over-fashioned page.
I could not say *I'm frightened* plain and true
without this scaffolding, this gilded cage.
The bird is real. I built the bars for you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
